analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax on large inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would eliminate the federal estate tax for heirs of very large fortunes, never received a hearing or vote and died in the Ways and Means Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the federal estate tax outright, meaning no tax at all on any inherited estate, no matter how large, for deaths after the end of 2022. It also keeps the "stepped-up basis" rule, which resets the value of inherited assets so heirs owe no capital-gains tax on growth that happened during the original owner's life. Only households with very large estates — above roughly $13 million per person under current law — pay any estate tax today. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates. Today the tax applies only after a per-person exemption of roughly $13 million, so a small fraction of the largest family fortunes — and the estate-planning industry that serves them — would gain the most. No one else currently pays this tax.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals chapter 11 of the Internal Revenue Code, the federal estate tax, effective for estates of people dying after December 31, 2022 [S2] [S3].

Retains "stepped-up basis" at death, so inherited assets are treated as newly purchased at their date-of-death value and heirs owe no capital-gains tax on gains accumulated during the original owner's lifetime — meaning large unrealized gains would escape tax entirely [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax raises revenue almost entirely from estates above roughly $13 million per person; repealing it would shift that burden to everyone else through higher deficits or other taxes, and the retention of stepped-up basis means heirs of large fortunes would owe no estate tax and no capital-gains tax on inherited gains.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone else through lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates federal revenue collected from the largest estates, shifting the burden onto other taxpayers or the deficit [S2].

Because the bill retains stepped-up basis, heirs would owe no tax of any kind on large unrealized gains — a fortune held in appreciated stock or land could pass entirely untaxed, generation after generation [S3].
The tax already exempts the first roughly $13 million per person, so repeal provides no benefit to any household below that threshold.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain is concentrated in a very small group — heirs to estates above roughly $13 million per person — while the cost is spread across everyone else as lost federal revenue. Because the bill keeps stepped-up basis, it goes further than repeal alone: large inherited fortunes would face no estate tax and no capital-gains tax, making it effectively a permanent tax shelter at the top of the wealth distribution.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Latta (R-OH) introduced the bill on January 12, 2023, with nine Republican cosponsors [S1] [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax remains on the books, so federal revenue from the largest estates continues. The heirs to very large fortunes and the estate-planning industry lost nothing by the bill's failure, but everyday taxpayers were spared the revenue loss that repeal would have spread to them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday taxpayers spared a revenue shift

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate tax and retain stepped-up basis [S1] [S3].

for.name: 9 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members joined [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters — the sponsor and nine cosponsors — were House Republicans; no Democrat joined, no hearing or vote was ever scheduled, and no recorded opposition appeared in the chamber record [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Heirs to very large estates (roughly $13 million-plus per person)
industries.note: Repeal would let the largest family fortunes pass entirely free of federal estate tax, and the retained stepped-up basis would also erase capital-gains tax on inherited gains. The revenue would instead fall on everyone else through deficits or other taxes.
Repealing the tax would eliminate the demand for estate-tax planning, shelters, and insurance strategies built around it.
